title: Rate-Fidelity Control for Wide-Area Quantum Links
authors: Connor Clayton, Cory Nunn, Quinn Carmack, Wayne McKenzie, Anne Marie Richards, Xiaodi Wu, Bobby Bhattacharjee
abstract: Quantum network links must distribute entanglement at high rates while satisfying application-specified fidelity demands. However, wide-area deployed fiber links suffer from polarization drift which destabilizes end-to-end fidelity and forces periodic compensation. Current deployments often use active stabilization with fixed control policies, and improvements generally stem from advances in quantum hardware. Meanwhile, software control remains relatively underexplored.   Here, we formulate quantum link operation as a joint control problem over tunable rate-fidelity tradeoffs and uncontrollable link drift. From this framework, we construct a link control protocol that dynamically adapts source pump power and polarization compensation to maximize entanglement distribution rate subject to a minimum fidelity constraint. We evaluate the protocol through trace-driven simulations driven by data from a 64 km deployed optical fiber. Compared with optimized static policies, our adaptive controller improves mean entanglement distribution rate by 14% over a 24 hour trace, without requiring any offline policy optimization. Our results show that software-based physical layer control can provide a practical mechanism for improving near-term quantum link performance without requiring additional quantum hardware.
summary: This paper introduces an adaptive control protocol designed to optimize entanglement distribution rates over long-haul quantum fiber links plagued by polarization drift. By treating the problem as a joint optimization of rate versus fidelity, the authors developed a software controller that dynamically adjusts source power and compensation timing. This approach significantly boosts performance in near-term quantum networks without requiring new physical hardware.
main_problem: The challenge is designing a control protocol for wide-area quantum links that maximizes entanglement distribution rate while ensuring the fidelity of transmitted quantum states remains above an application-specified threshold.
main_result: An adaptive, software-based controller was developed that improved the mean entanglement distribution rate by 14% over a 24-hour trace compared to optimized static policies.
method: The authors formulated the problem as a joint control optimization over tunable source parameters (pump power) and polarization compensation timing, using trace-driven simulations based on real fiber data.
model_or_system: The system models quantum communication over wide-area optical fiber links suffering from time-varying polarization drift. The control mechanism dynamically adjusts the entanglement source's pump power and applies polarization corrections to maintain high fidelity.
key_observables: Entanglement distribution rate, State Fidelity (F), Polarization State of Polarization (SOP).
important_parameters: 64 km deployed optical fiber length; minimum required fidelity threshold ($	ext{F}_{	ext{target}}$); pump laser power settings.
main_assumptions: The control protocol assumes that the link degradation can be modeled or predicted sufficiently well to guide adaptive adjustments, and it relies on classical processing rather than new quantum hardware.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the quantum link setup involving entanglement generation and polarization compensation measurements, the metropolitan context of the 64km fiber link, and rate-fidelity trade-offs for different sources.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical limitations (polarization drift) to formulating the problem as a joint control optimization. It then details the adaptive protocol construction, followed by rigorous evaluation using long-term trace simulations against static benchmarks.
why_interesting: This work provides a practical, software-defined solution for mitigating environmental decoherence in quantum networks, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics research concerning physical implementation challenges.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. (a) Schematic of our quantum link. Entanglement generation and automated polarization compensation (APC) signals are time multiplexed. Measurements at the APC receiver inform corrections at the polarization controller. (b) Feedback loop used for link control. Polarization fidelity (𝐹pol) measured by the APC acts as input to the link control protocol and its associated models, which in turn determine hardware parameters at the source site.

Fig. 2. Metropolitan context of the 64km deployed fiber link, part of the Washington DC metropolitan quantum network (DC-QNet). The source is located at the Laboratory for Telecommunication Sciences (LTS) in College Park, MD, USA. The route passes through a switch at the University of Maryland, then continues through a 62km partially-aerial fiber to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Gaithersburg, MD, USA. The exact routes of these two fibers are not known and therefore sketched as straight dashed lines.

Fig. 3. Schematic of experimental setup used to characterize SPDC entanglement source and receiver with controllable pump laser power. A complete diagram and its description can be found in Appendix A.

Fig. 4. Controllable rate-fidelity tradeoffs across two entanglement source technologies. In both sources, increasing pump power increases entanglement generation rate but reduces entanglement fidelity. The simulations in this paper use the SPDC characterization in (a).

Fig. 5. Measured polarization drift over 48 hours on a 64km fiber link. The top figure shows the evolution of raw Stokes parameters over time; the bottom plot shows the calculated drift rate averaged over 15 minute intervals. On average, drift is significantly higher during the day.
